Before mountains learned to stand still, they wandered the world like giant gray beasts, drinking from seas and sleeping beneath the stars. Among them was Orun, the smallest mountain, who carried a lantern of blue fire in a hollow of his chest.

Each night, Orun climbed the dark sky to light the moon, but the older mountains laughed. “You are too small to hold up heaven,” they rumbled. Ashamed, Orun hid his lantern in a valley, and the world fell into a night so deep that rivers forgot where to run and birds forgot their songs.

A child named Luma found the lantern and heard it whisper, “Light grows when it is shared.” She carried it to Orun and placed it back in his chest. Orun glowed brighter than dawn. Seeing this, the great mountains bowed, and their knees sank into the earth, where they remain today.

Orun rose highest of all, not because he was largest, but because he had carried the light. That is why the moon has a blue edge on winter nights, and why small hills shine after rain: they remember the mountain who taught the world that even a little flame can guide the dark home.

Before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of dark water, and above it drifted a lonely ember named Vey. Vey longed to see his own face, but there was nothing to shine upon. So he whispered to the water, “Lift one hand, and I will give you warmth.”

The water rose into a silver mountain. Vey touched its peak, and steam became clouds. From the clouds fell sparks, and each spark turned into a bird with a burning throat. Their songs cracked the darkness, and through the cracks came morning.

But the mountain grew proud. “I hold the sky,” it boasted. “All light belongs to me.” In anger, it shook off the birds, and their fiery feathers scattered across the heavens. Thus the stars were made.

Vey, saddened by pride, hid beneath the rim of the world. The birds searched for him every evening, calling with red and golden voices. When they nearly find him, the sky blushes. When they fail, night returns.

Yet each morning Vey forgives the mountain and climbs again, setting the waters glittering, waking the birds, and reminding all things that light is a gift, not a crown. The mountain listens in silence.

Myth: Before the earth had shadows, the sky was a closed shell and the seas slept without dreams. In that dimness drifted Vey, a small ember with a patient heart. He wished to wake the world, but his light was too lonely to spread.

So Vey sank into the sea and asked, “Who will rise with me?” A wave answered by lifting itself into a shining peak. Vey warmed it, and from its crown poured mist. The mist became birds of gold, each carrying a note of dawn beneath its tongue.

Their singing opened the shell of the sky. Morning spilled through, and the waters laughed for the first time. But the peak, seeing all creatures turn toward its brightness, grew proud. “I made the day,” it cried, and tried to cage the birds inside its stone hands.

The birds escaped, losing feathers as they flew. Those feathers became stars, scattered reminders of freedom. Vey, grieved, dimmed himself and hid beyond the western sea.

Now each evening the birds search for him, painting the clouds with fire. Each morning Vey returns, not to praise the mountain, but to warm it again, teaching that light shared freely becomes dawn, while light hoarded turns to stone. The sea keeps the lesson softly.

Myth: In the first dusk, before hills had roots, the mountains wandered like slow beasts across a world of sleeping water. Orun was the smallest, yet within his ribs he guarded a blue coal, the only memory of morning.

Each night he climbed the air and lifted it high, so fish could find the rivers and children could find their mothers. The greater peaks mocked him. Arvek, tallest and hardest, said, “Such fire belongs in a crown, not a hollow chest.” He shoved Orun, and the coal fell beneath the sea.

Darkness thickened. Birds swallowed their songs; waves forgot the shore. Then Luma, a girl with quiet hands, waded out and found the coal pulsing among shells. It burned her palms, but spoke gently: “Carry me to one who will share.”

She returned it to Orun. He shone without triumph, and his light softened even Arvek’s stone heart. The proud mountain knelt, sinking deep, and all his kin knelt after him, becoming the ranges of earth.

Since then, mountains cannot roam. They stand listening while Orun’s blue lantern rises, and dawn reddens their brows with remembered shame and hope for every small flame that teaches proud giants how to bow low.

Myth: Before dawn was counted, the world lay beneath a lid of black stone, and the sea dreamed without tides. In that stillness wandered Vey, a red ember no larger than a seed, carrying warmth he could not spend alone.

He called into the water, “Rise, and we will make a morning.” The sea lifted one shining hand, and it hardened into a mountain of pearl. Vey touched its summit. Steam curled upward, turning into bright-winged birds, and the birds sang so fiercely that cracks opened in the stone sky.

Through the cracks poured light. Rivers began to run, flowers unfolded, and every creature learned its color. The pearl mountain heard their praise and mistook it for worship. “I am the maker of day,” it boomed, closing its cliffs around the birds.

The birds burst free, scattering sparks from their wings. The sparks became stars, set high so no hand could imprison them. Vey, sorrowful but gentle, sank beyond the sea, leaving twilight behind him.

Each evening the birds follow his fading path, streaking the clouds with gold. Each morning he returns to warm the mountain’s cold face. Thus the world remembers: light grows by being shared, and even proud stone can be softened by patient fire. The sea hums this truth forever.
